title: Nice to meet you
goal: Greet people, say your name and where you're from, ask how someone is — and set up two habits from the very first sentence: the word "is/am/are" that can never be skipped, and the verb that always comes last.
bekal: greet and say goodbye in two registers, formal and casual
give your name, where you're from, and your nationality in full sentences
use the four forms of "to be": ہوں، ہے، ہو، ہیں

dialogs.title: مکالمہ — لاہور ایئرپورٹ پر
dialogs.intro: Budi has just landed in Lahore. Someone is waiting for him at the exit, holding a slip of paper.

lines.speaker: بودی:
lines.text: جی ہاں، میں بودی ہوں۔ آپ کا نام کیا ہے؟
lines.baca: jī hāñ, maiñ Būdī hūñ. āp kā nām kyā hai?
lines.id: Yes, I'm Budi. What's your name?
lines.literal: yes yes, I Budi am. you of name what is?

lines.speaker: علی:
lines.text: میرا نام علی ہے۔ خوش آمدید!
lines.baca: merā nām Alī hai. ḵush āmdīd!
lines.literal: my name Ali is. happy come!

lines.speaker: علی:
lines.text: میں ٹھیک ہوں، شکریہ۔ اور آپ؟
lines.baca: maiñ ṭhīk hūñ, shukriya. aur āp?
lines.id: I'm fine, thank you. And you?
lines.literal: I fine am, thanks. and you?

lines.speaker: بودی:
lines.text: میں انڈونیشیا سے ہوں۔ کیا آپ پاکستانی ہیں؟
lines.baca: maiñ Inḍonesiyā se hūñ. kyā āp Pākistānī haiñ?
lines.id: I'm from Indonesia. Are you Pakistani?
lines.literal: I Indonesia from am. Q you Pakistan-i are?

lines.speaker: علی:
lines.text: جی، میں لاہور سے ہوں۔ آپ سے مل کر خوشی ہوئی۔
lines.baca: jī, maiñ Lāhaur se hūñ. āp se mil kar ḵushī huī.
lines.id: Yes, I'm from Lahore. Nice to meet you.
lines.literal: yes, I Lahore from am. you with having-met happiness happened.

notes: **The word "is/am/are" is required, and it goes last.** English already insists on it — "I *am* Budi" — but Urdu also moves it: میں بودی ہوں, with ہوں (*hūñ*) sitting at the **very end** of the sentence, not in the middle. Two habits at once, and both start today.

**One word کیا, two completely different jobs.** At the **start** of a sentence it isn't a word at all but a spoken question mark: کیا آپ بودی ہیں؟ = "Are you Budi?". **Inside** the sentence it means "what": آپ کا نام کیا ہے؟ = "what is your name?". Position tells them apart, not form.

**A single syllable جی that makes everything polite.** On its own, جی means "yes". Paired, it softens: جی ہاں (yes, politely), جی نہیں (no, politely). Said with a rising tone, جی؟ means "sorry, what?". And after a name it's a mark of respect: علی جی. Pakistanis use it dozens of times a day; copying them makes your Urdu sound instantly more grown-up.

**"Thank you" is شکریہ.** It comes from the same Arabic root as *shukran*, "thanks". The reply: کوئی بات نہیں (*koī bāt nahīñ*, "no problem") or, warmer, خوشی ہوئی ("my pleasure"). For extra gratitude: بہت بہت شکریہ.

**Look closely at آپ سے مل کر خوشی ہوئی.** Literally "you with having met, happiness happened". Notice that سے ("with") comes **after** آپ, not before it. Every Urdu preposition works this way — they're postpositions — and unit 6 is devoted to them.

**Saying goodbye: اللہ حافظ or خدا حافظ?** Both mean "may God protect you" and both are used. The older خدا حافظ (*ḵudā hāfiz*) uses the Persian word for God and is used by everyone, including non-Muslim Urdu speakers; اللہ حافظ has spread in Pakistan since the 1980s. If you're unsure in front of someone you don't know, choose **خدا حافظ** — it's never wrong. The most casual: پھر ملیں گے ("see you again").

grammars.title: The four forms of "to be"
body: Urdu has one verb "to be" — ہونا (*honā*) — and its form changes with the person speaking or spoken about, much like English *am/is/are*. These four forms cover everyday conversation, and you'll need them in every unit from here on.
The good news: they **don't change for gender**. Men and women alike say میں ہوں. Gender arrives in unit 2, not here.
after: To make it negative, add one word: **نہیں** (*nahīñ*). میں ڈاکٹر نہیں ہوں = "I'm not a doctor". Note the position — نہیں goes right **before** ہوں, not at the front of the sentence.

grammars.title: The Urdu verb goes last
body: This is the most basic difference in word order between English and Urdu, and spotting it now saves months of muddle. English puts the verb in the middle: *I drink tea*. Urdu puts it at the **end**: میں چائے پیتا ہوں — literally "I tea drinking-am".
The practical rule fits in one sentence: **whatever you say, the verb goes in last.** Everything else — subject, time, place, object — lines up in front of it.
after: A small exercise that helps enormously in the first week: before translating any sentence into Urdu, **write the verb at the far right of the page first**, then fill in the rest from right to left. After two weeks your head does it on its own.

head: Urdu
Say it
When to use it
rows: The most common greeting in Pakistan, any time, to anyone.
A refined greeting across religions, originally from Lucknow. Used by Muslims and non-Muslims alike, and it sounds cultured.
"Hello". Very common in big cities, especially on the phone.
Good morning. Somewhat formal; in daily life people still say السلام علیکم.
Good night, when parting to go to sleep.
See you again. Casual and warm.

blocks.text: Three words for "you", and how to choose
Urdu makes you choose a level of politeness in every sentence, and that choice carries all the way into the verb. For now, memorize just one rule and you'll never offend anyone.

head: Form
To whom
Verb
rows: **Always use this one.** New people, older people, your boss, shopkeepers, anyone you're not close to.
Close friends your own age, younger siblings, children.
Very intimate: to small children, or to God in prayer. To an adult who isn't a close relative, it's **rude**.

blocks.title: When in doubt, آپ — it costs you nothing
items: Using آپ with a close friend only sounds a little stiff, and they'll laugh and tell you to use تم. Using تو with someone you've just met sounds **insulting**, and no one will tell you to stop — they'll just keep their distance.
The switch from آپ to تم is usually offered by the older or more senior person: تم کہہ سکتے ہو ("you can say *tum*"). Wait for that offer.
There is one place where تو is always right: in prayer. That's why Urdu prayers say تو ہی — "only You".

blocks.title: Yes/no questions — just put کیا in front
items: A statement: آپ پاکستانی ہیں۔ ("You are Pakistani.") A question: **کیا** آپ پاکستانی ہیں؟ Nothing is taken apart, no words swap places — just one کیا at the front.
In casual speech the کیا is often **dropped**, and only a rising tone at the end marks the question: آپ پاکستانی ہیں؟ Just like "You're Pakistani?" in English.
Answers: جی ہاں (yes) · جی نہیں (no) · شاید (maybe) · بالکل (absolutely).
